content: I'll start by reading the test image to analyze the visual symptoms.

The test image shows:
- A tomato plant stem pulled from the ground and split open longitudinally
- **White cottony/mycelial growth** visible on the outer stem near the soil line
- Internal pith/vascular tissue exposed, appearing yellow-white
- Plant is dead/wilted with brown, dried leaves
- Image taken at soil level showing root crown area

Key features: white mycelium at soil line + stem rot + whole plant collapse. Top candidates: **Southern_Blight**, **Sclerotinia_Timber_Rot**, **Verticillium_Wilt**, **Southern_Bacterial_Wilt**.

Now I'll view one reference image from each of my top 4 candidates.
This Southern Blight reference is a field overview shot. Let me check Sclerotinia Timber Rot next.
The Sclerotinia reference shows white mycelium with dark sclerotia bodies on stems. Now let me check Verticillium Wilt.
Verticillium Wilt shows yellowing leaves, not matching the stem-splitting with white mycelium. Let me check Southern Blight's more detailed reference.

Excellent comparison. The Southern Blight reference (Bugwood_55) shows a plant in **sandy soil** with **complete stem collapse at soil line** — very consistent with the test image's setting and symptom pattern.

**Analysis summary:**

| Feature | Test Image | Best Match |
|---|---|---|
| White cottony mycelium on stem base | Yes, clearly visible | Southern Blight ✓ |
| Stem girdling/rot at soil line | Yes, stem split at ground level | Southern Blight ✓ |
| Complete plant collapse/wilt | Yes, all leaves brown/dead | Southern Blight ✓ |
| Sandy soil environment | Yes | Southern Blight ✓ |
| Dark sclerotia visible | Not clearly | Sclerotinia less likely |

The test image shows white mycelial growth on the outer stem at/near soil line with the stem pulled up and split — classic Southern Blight (Sclerotium rolfsii) presentation. The Sclerotinia reference had visible large black sclerotia not present in the test image. Verticillium showed vascular discoloration without surface mycelium. Southern Bacterial Wilt would show bacterial streaming, not fungal growth.
